newsitem.title: UK: Black and Jewish not enough for London's Bengalis.
newsitem.headline: Black and Jewish not enough for London's Bengalis.

text.p: Oona King is black and Jewish but that cuts little ice with many of the voters in the inner-city east London constituency where she is standing for the opposition Labour Party.

With Labour well ahead in opinion polls, King can expect to inherit the seat of Bethnal Green and Bow from Peter Shore, who is retiring after more than three decades representing the area and will bequeath her a strong 12,000 vote majority.
If she is successful in the May 1 general election, the 29-year-old King will become Britain's second black woman member of parliament, representing one of the poorest constituencies in the country.

But with about 28 percent of the population of the constituency of Bangladeshi origin, the vocal Bengali community had felt it should provide the next Labour member of parliament, especially as no Bengali has yet sat in the House of Commons.

As if to ram home the message, the call to prayer rang out from a nearby mosque as Labour Party members arrived for the meeting on Thursday at which King was to be formally adopted as their candidate.
Questioned closely by Bengali journalists, King said she would work hard for the constituency, but insisted she had won the vote at the earlier meeting that chose the Labour candidate.
"I appreciate the problems that have been caused by my selection," she told a news conference. "I got the largest number of votes and I can't apologise for the fact that I won at that meeting."

Glenys Kinnock, a member of the European parliament and wife of former British Labour Party leader Neil Kinnock, employed King as an assistant at the European parliament and has turned out to help her former employee's election campaign.

She acknowledged that King had difficulties in a constituency where the Conservative and Liberal Democrats had put up Bengali candidates, but insisted that the Bengali community would rally round King.
"I've had a sense of the warmth and generosity of the people towards her. What happened before is in the past."
King told one Bengali questioner that she had been upbraided by the Conservative candidate, Syed Nurul Islam, for being unable to speak his language and not coming from his country.
She had replied that he sounded like a representative of the hardline nationalist British National Party.

The BNP has found an echo in London's East End, where white residents often resent growing immigrant numbers. King says the BNP has moved a candidate with the same name -- David King -- into the constituency as a spoiling tactic.
If King does take her seat after the election, she may not be warmly welcomed into the House of Commons by Diane Abbott, the first and only black woman MP.
Media reports say that after a row over an attempt by King to be selected to stand for Abbott's Hackney constituency in north London, the two are in a state of "armed neutrality".
